passage: The Christmas holidays were two days away, and the bus stop outside the panchayat school in Kuttanad was crowded and loud. Joseph arrived in an enormous brown sweater, sleeves folded three times. Someone shouted, "Appooppan sweater! Grandpa sweater!" Then five voices, then ten. Seema was in the middle of the knot of kids, and before she knew it her voice was in the chant too, loud and laughing. Nobody could tell which voice was hers. Joseph stared at the road. On the bus, Seema sat alone by the window. She would never have said it to Joseph by herself; last month he had shared his umbrella with her all the way home. Her stomach felt sour the whole ride.

qa.q: How many times were Joseph's sleeves folded?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: How did Seema feel on the bus afterwards?
qa.a: She felt guilty and uneasy, her stomach sour, because she had joined a chant she would never have said to Joseph alone.

qa.q: What could Seema do next?
qa.a: She could say sorry to Joseph, and next time step out of the chant or tell the others to stop instead of hiding in the crowd.

qa.q: What was it like for Joseph at the bus stop?
qa.a: It was likely humiliating and lonely to face ten laughing voices with no one to reason with, so he just stared at the road.

grounding: A child in a noisy group at a bus stop joins teasing she would never do alone, because in the crowd nobody can tell which voice is hers.

subtype: Behind a screen or in a mob [Actor]
passage: Over the Diwali holidays, someone made an anonymous page for mocking people's videos from our class, and everyone commented under fake names. When Trisha's dance video went up, the comments piled on: remarks about her voice, her dress, rows of laughing faces. I had a fake account called sparkler_99. I typed one line, something about her dancing like a wobbling jelly, and hit post. It didn't feel like me doing it. It felt like the page doing it. Two days later, at the colony Diwali party, Trisha stood near the rangoli, not dancing, not eating. Seeing her face made my line mine again. That night I deleted the account, sent Trisha a real apology signed with my real name, Shalini, and told Ma. The next morning Ma and I showed the page to our class teacher, who reported it to the school the same day.

qa.q: What was the name of the fake account?
qa.a: sparkler_99.

qa.q: Why did the post not feel like Shalini's own at first?
qa.a: Hidden behind a fake name among many comments, Shalini felt distant and unaccountable, as if the page wrote it, until seeing Trisha brought on shame.

qa.q: Which of Shalini's steps set things right, and why?
qa.a: Deleting the account, apologising with a real name, and telling Ma and the class teacher, because it took responsibility and got the page stopped.

qa.q: What was the Diwali party like for Trisha?
qa.a: It was probably painful and lonely; Trisha stood apart by the rangoli, not dancing or eating, after the pile-on.

grounding: A teenager behind a fake account joins an online pile-on because the target feels distant and everyone is doing it, then takes the act back as their own.

passage:
Vaibhav: new year's eve and i'm in hell. are u seeing the new group
Elizabeth: which one
Vaibhav: someone added me to "Vaibhav fan club". 43 people. i don't know half the numbers
Vaibhav: they keep posting my class photo with stuff written on it. more every minute
Elizabeth: who made it??
Vaibhav: no idea. i typed "please stop" and got 30 replies laughing
Vaibhav: i can't even argue. there's no one person. it's like shouting at a wave
Elizabeth: screenshot first. then leave the group. don't reply
Elizabeth: and tell your dad NOW, not tomorrow. please
Vaibhav: ok
[9:40 pm]
Vaibhav: told Papa. he read all of it and said it's not my fault. we saved the screenshots and he emailed the principal and class teacher. he's sitting with me
Elizabeth: good. i'm here too

qa.q: How many people were in the group Vaibhav was added to?
qa.a: 43 people.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav feel as the messages keep coming?
qa.a: He feels overwhelmed and helpless, because there is no one person to reason with; it's like shouting at a wave.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth advise, and why was it wise?
qa.a: To screenshot, leave the group, not reply and tell his dad right away, which keeps evidence and gets an adult involved the same night.

qa.q: How might Papa feel reading the messages?
qa.a: Papa likely feels upset and protective, but he stays calm, tells Vaibhav it is not his fault and acts at once.

grounding: A student mobbed by dozens of messages in a group feels overwhelmed because there is no single person to reason with.

subtype: Noticing the slide in a group [Observer]
passage: The college had won the inter-university cricket final, and by ten the hostel road was a party: drums, dancing, someone's speaker blasting songs. Then the rain started, and the mood changed. A group began rocking a parked scooter for fun. Somebody lit a string of crackers and threw it toward the watchman's cabin. The crowd roared. Kalyani, near the gate, felt her chest go tight. These were the same people who had queued politely in the mess that morning. Now they were laughing at things they would hate to see on video tomorrow. Worse, she couldn't find Uma, who had gone to buy chai. Kalyani texted: where r u, it's getting bad. Then she tapped two friends near the scooter. "Guys. Enough. The watchman's inside." One of them blinked, as if waking up, and stepped back. Uma appeared, soaked, and the two of them walked back to the hostel together.

qa.q: What did the group start rocking?
qa.a: A parked scooter.

qa.q: What did Kalyani feel as the crackers were thrown toward the cabin?
qa.a: She felt alarmed, her chest tight, seeing people who were polite that morning now acting in ways they would regret.

qa.q: What did Kalyani do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She tapped two friends and reminded them the watchman was inside, which made one step back as if waking up, and then she found Uma and left.

qa.q: How might the friend who stepped back feel the next day?
qa.a: That friend might feel relieved and a little ashamed, glad to have been stopped before something worse happened.

grounding: A young adult at a victory celebration sees the mood slide from festive to reckless, calms two friends and leaves.

subtype: Keeping the self in the crowd [Response]
passage: At 11 pm, with a client deck due by 9 the next morning, Arohi's phone kept buzzing with the team's after-hours chat. It had started as jokes about the deadline. Then someone posted a clip of Himani, the new analyst, stumbling over a word in her first client call, with the voice slowed down. Laughing faces flooded in. "Arohi?? Your turn," someone tagged her. Arohi's thumb hovered. It would be easy; nobody would remember who sent what. But the name above the message would be hers, tomorrow and every day after. She typed, in her own words: "Not for me. She's two weeks in and it was a hard call. Let's delete this." Then she muted the chat, went back to slide 14, and later sent Himani a private note: "Your client call was fine. First ones are always rough."

qa.q: By what time was the client deck due?
qa.a: By 9 the next morning.

qa.q: What went through Arohi's mind as her thumb hovered?
qa.a: She felt tempted, since nobody would remember who sent what, but uneasy knowing the message would carry her name every day after.

qa.q: Which of Arohi's choices would help anyone in a similar chat?
qa.a: Answering in her own words, asking the group to delete the clip, and privately reassuring Himani keep accountability even in a crowd.

qa.q: What would change for Himani if Arohi had joined in?
qa.a: The pile-on would grow and Himani might feel mocked by the whole team, instead of getting one kind private note.

grounding: A young professional in a team chat remembers her name travels with her words, refuses to join mockery of a new colleague and steps back.

passage:
Monday, the first day after the winter break. Sonali is made class monitor. She blushes, promises to be fair, and helps Sudha carry the register.
Thursday. Sonali stands at the front with the duster, writing names of talkers on the board. "Sudha, name. Rohit, name." When Sudha says she was only asking for a pen, Sonali snaps, "Complaints after class." She likes how the room goes quiet when she raises her hand.
The next Tuesday. Nobody asks Sonali to sit with them at lunch. On the board she has listed eleven names, and she hasn't once asked why anyone was talking. Sudha passes her a folded note: "You were nicer before." Sonali crumples it, then, slowly, smooths it out again.

qa.q: How many names had Sonali listed on the board by the next Tuesday?
qa.a: Eleven names.

qa.q: What does Sonali enjoy on Thursday, and what does that suggest?
qa.a: She enjoys how the room goes quiet when she raises her hand, which suggests she feels powerful and pleased at being obeyed and stops caring about reasons.

qa.q: What could Sonali try after reading Sudha's note?
qa.a: She could ask why people are talking before writing names, and hear complaints straight away, as she promised on the first day.

qa.q: How does Sudha feel about Sonali's change?
qa.a: Sudha feels hurt and let down, since she only asked for a pen and still got her name on the board.

grounding: A teenager made class monitor starts enjoying being obeyed, bosses classmates and brushes off their complaints.

passage:
Dear Parul,
Happy Navratri! Our hostel did garba in the courtyard, and as general secretary I got to open it. Very filmy, I know.
Honestly, being GS is exhausting. The first-years keep coming to my room about the mess food and the broken geysers. I told them to put it in writing and stop whining; we all survived first year. One of them started crying in the corridor, which, really, was a bit much.
Best perk: committee members can come back after the 10 pm curfew "for meetings". I've used it three times this week, twice just for chai at the bus stand. The warden never checks.
Don't worry, Parul, I'm still the same Salma who cried at our school farewell. Power hasn't gone to my head, ha!
Write soon,
Salma

qa.q: How many times did Salma use the late-return perk this week?
qa.a: Three times, twice just for chai at the bus stand.

qa.q: How does Salma seem to feel about the first-years' complaints?
qa.a: Salma seems irritated and dismissive, calling the crying a bit much, without noticing how upset the juniors are.

qa.q: What could Salma do if Parul points out the change?
qa.a: Salma could go back and hear the first-years' mess and geyser complaints properly, and stop using the curfew exception for chai.

qa.q: How might the first-year who cried in the corridor see Salma?
qa.a: That student probably sees a cold senior who brushes off real problems, not the kind person Salma believes is still there.

grounding: A student leader stops noticing how juniors feel and bends the curfew rule for personal chai, while believing nothing has changed.

passage: The Holi week before the March closing was when I noticed how small I had become. By then I could read Bidisha ma'am's moods from the corridor: heels fast meant don't speak; phone face down meant maybe. I had a real doubt about the new vendor numbers. In my head I rehearsed saying it three times. In the meeting she asked, "All fine, Gautam?" and I heard myself say, "Yes, ma'am, all good." Everyone nodded. We all did that. At the office Holi lunch, colours everywhere, I laughed at her jokes a beat too early. On the bus home, pink powder still on my collar, I thought about the college Gautam who argued with professors for fun. I didn't know where that person had gone. I only knew I had got very good at being quiet.

qa.q: What did fast heels in the corridor mean to Gautam?
qa.a: Don't speak.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel on the bus home?
qa.a: Gautam felt small and a little sad, missing the college self who argued for fun and seeing how watchful and quiet work had made that self.

qa.q: What small step could Gautam try about the vendor numbers?
qa.a: Gautam could write the doubt down with the figures and send it to Bidisha ma'am, which may be easier than saying it in a tense meeting.

qa.q: What might Bidisha ma'am be missing when everyone says "all good"?
qa.a: She might be missing real problems like the vendor numbers, because her team only tells her what pleases her.

grounding: A junior employee learns to read a powerful manager's moods and say only what pleases, and feels smaller for it.

passage:
"Sarika, got five minutes?" Elizabeth set two coffees down in the pantry.
"Three. The quarterly review."
"That's sort of what I wanted to talk about. Can I say something as your friend, not your team member?"
Sarika sighed. "Go on."
"In yesterday's stand-up you cut Nikhil off twice. And last week you asked me to swap my leave because yours 'mattered more'. That isn't the Sarika who used to cover my shifts."
"You don't know what it's like. Everyone wants something from me. The director calls at eleven at night."
"I believe you. The pressure's real. I'm not saying this to anyone else. I just miss how you used to listen."
Sarika stared into the coffee. "I cut Nikhil off twice?"
"Twice."
"...I'll talk to him."

qa.q: How many times did Sarika cut Nikhil off?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: Why does Elizabeth say this is not being said to anyone else?
qa.a: Elizabeth feels caring and a bit anxious, wanting Sarika to hear it as a friend's concern, not gossip.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth get right in raising the change?
qa.a: Elizabeth gave concrete examples, spoke privately as a friend and accepted that the pressure is real, so Sarika could listen instead of defending.

qa.q: What is it like for Sarika to hear this?
qa.a: It is uncomfortable at first, and Sarika defends with the director's late calls, but the specific examples lead to surprise and a plan to talk to Nikhil.

grounding: A peer sees a friend turned manager stop listening and expect special treatment, and names it gently in private while granting the pressure is real.

passage: Omkar was twenty-six and the youngest head chef the hotel kitchen had ever had. Every Friday after the dinner rush, he pulled up an upturned crate and asked the same question: "What did I get wrong this week?" The first month, nobody answered. Then Jagdish, the oldest cook, said, "The new 6 am prep shift. You didn't ask who takes the first bus." Three of the dishwashers came from villages an hour away. Omkar went quiet, then moved prep to seven. When a food critic praised the new mango kulfi, Omkar pointed at the pastry section. "Ask Lata. It's her recipe." Some nights he rang an old friend from catering college who never let him win an argument. "Still humble, chef?" "Trying," Omkar said.

qa.q: What time did Omkar move the prep shift to?
qa.a: Seven.

qa.q: Why did Omkar go quiet after Jagdish spoke?
qa.a: He felt surprised and a little ashamed to realise his 6 am shift had cost the dishwashers who took the first bus, and he wanted to fix it.

qa.q: Which of Omkar's habits guard against self-importance?
qa.a: Asking every Friday what he got wrong, crediting Lata for the kulfi, and keeping a friend who argues with him all keep him curious about others.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel after the prep shift moved?
qa.a: Jagdish would likely feel respected and trusted, seeing that honest feedback to the young chef actually changed things.

grounding: A young head chef invites honest feedback, asks what his decisions cost his staff, shares credit and keeps a friend who disagrees.
